**Treaty of Waitangi**
The 1840 treaty signed by British representative William Hobson and more than 500 Maori chiefs (rangatira), which made New Zealand a British colony with Hobson as its first governor. Its English and Maori versions differ, most notably in how the word "sovereignty" was translated, and the dispute over its terms fueled later conflicts and land claims.

**Musket Wars**
A series of early 19th-century wars among Maori tribes (iwi), made far deadlier by European firearms. The Ngapuhi chief Hongi Hika acquired muskets and launched raids as far as Lake Rotorua and the Bay of Plenty. Maori adapted their hillforts into "gunfighter" pa to cope with the new weapons.

**Flagstaff War and Hone Heke**
An 1845–1846 conflict begun when the Ngapuhi chief Hone Heke, Hongi Hika's nephew, repeatedly cut down the British flagstaff at Kororareka (Russell). The flagstaff had been a gift from Heke to British Resident James Busby, who helped draft the Treaty of Waitangi. The war featured sieges of fortified pa.

**Maori**
The Polynesian indigenous people of New Zealand, who call the country Aotearoa. Their ancestors arrived by canoe, according to legend led by Kupe the Navigator, bringing the kumara (sweet potato). They built hillforts called pa, perform the haka war dance (made famous by the All Blacks rugby team), and call white settlers "Pakeha."

**First women's suffrage (1893)**
In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to give all women the right to vote in national elections.

**Rogernomics and Ruthanasia**
Rogernomics was the free-market program of deregulation and restructuring pushed by Finance Minister Roger Douglas in David Lange's Fourth Labour Government from 1984. Its harsher continuation under National Party finance minister Ruth Richardson in the early 1990s was nicknamed "Ruthanasia."

**Robert Muldoon and the "Schnapps Election"**
Muldoon was a National Party prime minister (1975–1984) who promoted large state-funded industrial projects under the "Think Big" strategy. After losing a vote over nuclear policy, he called the snap 1984 election on live television while visibly drunk, and he lost it to David Lange.

**Sinking of the Rainbow Warrior**
In 1985 agents of the French intelligence service DGSE bombed the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbor, in an attack code-named Operation Satanic, to stop its protests against French nuclear testing in Polynesia. Photographer Fernando Pereira was killed. The attack strengthened New Zealand's anti-nuclear stance under David Lange.

**1981 Springbok Tour**
Muldoon allowed South Africa's apartheid-era national rugby team, the Springboks, to tour New Zealand, which critics said broke the Gleneagles Agreement against sporting contact with South Africa. Massive protests followed, including clashes on Molesworth Street and a light plane dropping flour bombs on the field during a match.

**New Zealand Wars (Maori Wars or Land Wars)**
A series of 19th-century wars between British colonial forces and Maori over land and sovereignty. They include the Hutt Valley campaign under Governor George Grey, the Waikato War against the Maori King Movement, the Battle of Gate Pa, where Maori defeated General Duncan Cameron, and later guerrilla campaigns led by Te Kooti and Titokowaru.

**Boyd Massacre**
In 1809, after Te Ara, the son of a Maori chief, was flogged aboard the ship Boyd, Maori at Whangaroa Harbour killed and ate most of the crew and passengers. The event discouraged European contact with Maori for years afterward.

**Abel Tasman**
The Dutch explorer who in 1642 became the first European to see New Zealand and encounter the Maori. James Cook later mapped the islands, and Cook Strait between the North and South Islands is named for him.

**ANZAC and Gallipoli**
The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps was formed in World War I and suffered heavy casualties in the 1915 Gallipoli campaign against the Ottoman Empire.

**New Zealand Company and Edward Gibbon Wakefield**
A colonization company founded on the plans of Edward Gibbon Wakefield, who had earlier promoted settlement in South Australia. It sent the ship Tory to New Zealand in 1839 to buy land, and its settlers founded Wellington. A land dispute involving its settlers led to the 1843 Wairau Affray with Te Rauparaha's Ngati Toa.

**Moriori massacre in the Chatham Islands**
In 1835 Maori groups displaced during the Musket Wars invaded the Chatham Islands and killed or enslaved many of the peaceful Moriori people living there.
